name.text: Calculating probabilities of non-mutually exclusive events in a sports day

questiontext.text:
At a sports day for {@school@}, there are exactly {@N@} learners in Form 3. The games master records the following participation data:

  • {@R@} learners entered running events (\(R\)).
  • {@F@} learners entered field events (\(F\)).
  • {@B@} learners entered both running and field events.

a) If one learner is selected at random, find the probability that they entered both running and field events.

(Enter your answer as a fully simplified fraction).

\(P(R \text{ and } F) =\) [[input:ans1]]

[[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

b) Because the events \(R\) and \(F\) can happen at the same time, they are not mutually exclusive. Find the probability that the selected learner entered running events OR field events.

\(P(R \text{ or } F) =\) [[input:ans2]]

[[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

c) Let \(E_1\) be the event "entered running events ONLY" and \(E_2\) be the event "entered field events ONLY". Because a learner cannot be in the "only running" group and the "only field" group simultaneously, \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) are mutually exclusive.

Find the probability that the learner entered exactly one type of event (\(E_1 \text{ or } E_2\)).

\(P(E_1 \text{ or } E_2) =\) [[input:ans3]]

[[validation:ans3]] [[feedback:prt3]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution:

Part a: Joint Probability
There are \({@B@}\) learners who entered both events, out of a total of \({@N@}\) learners.

\( \displaystyle P(R \text{ and } F) = \frac{{@B@}}{{@N@}} \)

\( \displaystyle \boxed{ P(R \text{ and } F) = {@ta1@} } \)

Part b: General Addition Rule
To find the probability of \(R \text{ or } F\), we must add the individual probabilities and subtract the intersection so we do not count the learners who did both twice:

\( \displaystyle P(R \text{ or } F) = P(R) + P(F) - P(R \text{ and } F) \)

\( \displaystyle P(R \text{ or } F) = \frac{{@R@}}{{@N@}} + \frac{{@F@}}{{@N@}} - \frac{{@B@}}{{@N@}} \)

\( \displaystyle P(R \text{ or } F) = \frac{{@R + F - B@}}{{@N@}} \)

\( \displaystyle \boxed{ P(R \text{ or } F) = {@ta2@} } \)

Part c: Mutually Exclusive Sub-Events
First, we find the number of learners in each exclusive group:

  • Running ONLY = Total Running - Both = \({@R@} - {@B@} = {@R_only@}\)
  • Field ONLY = Total Field - Both = \({@F@} - {@B@} = {@F_only@}\)

Because these are mutually exclusive, we can simply add their probabilities together:

\( \displaystyle P(E_1 \text{ or } E_2) = P(E_1) + P(E_2) \)

\( \displaystyle P(E_1 \text{ or } E_2) = \frac{{@R_only@}}{{@N@}} + \frac{{@F_only@}}{{@N@}} = \frac{{@R_only + F_only@}}{{@N@}} \)

\( \displaystyle \boxed{ P(E_1 \text{ or } E_2) = {@ta3@} } \)

The Venn diagram shows the four groups of learners:

questiondescription.text:
This question is based on the example Non-Mutually Exclusive Events in the section Mutually Exclusive and Independent Events of the CBC Grade 11 Mathematics textbook (INNODEMS).

Mutually Exclusive Events and the Addition Rule

truefeedback.text: Correct. The probability of the intersection is simply the number of learners who did both divided by the total population.

falsefeedback.text: Incorrect. Identify the specific number of learners who entered both events, and divide it by the total number of learners in Form 3.

truefeedback.text: Excellent. You correctly subtracted the intersection to avoid double-counting.

node.description: Check if they double-counted the intersection

truefeedback.text: You simply added \(P(R) + P(F)\). Because the events are not mutually exclusive, adding them directly means you counted the \({@B@}\) learners who did both events twice. You must subtract \(P(R \text{ and } F)\) from your total.

falsefeedback.text: Incorrect. Use the general addition rule: \(P(R \text{ or } F) = P(R) + P(F) - P(R \text{ and } F)\).

node.description: Algebraic equivalence of mutually exclusive union

truefeedback.text: Correct. Because \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) are mutually exclusive, you can directly add their probabilities without subtracting an intersection.

falsefeedback.text: Incorrect. First, find how many learners did only running (\({@R@} - {@B@}\)). Then, find how many did only field events (\({@F@} - {@B@}\)). Add these two groups together and divide by the total number of learners.
